1. **Statutory and EU framework**

- Regulation 5(1), Part-time Workers (Prevention of Less Favourable Treatment) Regulations 2000:
  - A part-time worker has the right not to be treated less favourably than a comparable full-time worker **“on the ground that”** they work part-time, unless objectively justified.
- Regulation 5(2):
  - Less favourable treatment is not unlawful if it is objectively justified on grounds other than the worker’s part-time status (legitimate aim; proportionate means).
- Directive 97/81/EC and the Framework Agreement, cl. 4(1):
  - Part-time workers shall not be treated less favourably than comparable full-time workers **“solely because”** they work part-time, unless justified on objective grounds.
  - Cl. 4(2) adds the **pro rata temporis** principle.

The UK Regulations must be interpreted, so far as possible, consistently with the Directive and Framework Agreement.

2. **How should “on the ground that” / “solely because” be interpreted?**

(a) **Analogy with UK discrimination law**

UK courts have long held in other discrimination contexts that phrases such as “on the grounds of” (sex, race, etc.):

- Do **not** require the protected characteristic to be the **sole** or even the main reason.
- It is enough that the characteristic is an **effective and significant cause** of the treatment:
  - See e.g. *Nagarajan v London Regional Transport* [1999] (House of Lords) on “on racial grounds”.

If “on the ground that” in the 2000 Regulations were interpreted as “sole reason only”, the protection would be drastically weakened: an employer could always point to some additional motive (e.g. “cost-saving”) to defeat liability at the threshold. That is the very argument the House of Lords rejected in *Nagarajan*.

(b) **Reconciling “solely because” in the Framework Agreement**

The Framework Agreement says “solely because they work part-time” **and** separately allows different treatment that is “justified on objective grounds”.

If “solely because” were read as “the only reason in the employer’s mind”, the objective justification defence would be largely redundant: the employer would defeat the claim simply by pointing to any additional reason, without going through a justification analysis at all.

A more coherent reading (and the one consistent with other EU equality instruments) is:

- The prohibition catches any less favourable treatment **because of** part-time status (where that status is an effective cause), and
- The reference to “solely because” is there to distinguish:
  - treatment grounded in the worker’s part-time status itself; from
  - treatment grounded in objectively justified, non-status-related reasons.

That is exactly what Regulation 5 implements: the claimant proves less favourable treatment **on the ground of** part-time status; then the employer can justify that treatment **on grounds other than** part-time status.

Hence, an English court, constraining itself to EU-conform interpretation and existing discrimination law logic, should hold:

- A claimant **does not** need to prove that part-time status was the **only** reason.
- It is sufficient that part-time status was **one effective and operative reason** for the less favourable treatment.

3. **Applying that interpretation to Reeves**

From the facts:

- Both parties **accept** that Reeves’s part-time status **was a factor** in the treatment complained of.
- The dispute is whether it had to be the **sole** basis.

Under the correct legal test (one effective reason is enough), that concession is very significant:

- Once it is accepted that part-time status was a real operative reason, the “on the ground that” element is, in principle, satisfied.

4. **Is there “less favourable treatment”?**

- Comparator: a full-time driver doing the same or broadly similar work for Stone Rides Inc.
- Treatment complained of: a flat “circuit fee” charged equally to all drivers for access to the booking system.

Although the contractual term is formally identical, in practice:

- A full-time driver will typically obtain more work and earnings for the same fixed fee.
- A part-time driver like Reeves gets fewer bookings and thus bears a **higher effective cost per hour/booking**.

The courts in other part-time worker and equal pay cases have been willing to look at the **real effect** of terms and not mere formal symmetry (e.g. *British Airways plc v Pinaud* in relation to availability vs. pay).

In substance, the requirement to pay a non‑pro‑rated, flat fee for the same “access” is **less favourable to part-time workers**, contrary to the pro rata temporis principle, because:

- The financial burden of the fee is significantly greater, relative to the amount of work, for part-timers than for full-timers.

Thus, there is a plausible finding of less favourable treatment in “employment conditions” when measured in practice, not just on paper.

5. **Causation: is the treatment “on the ground” of part-time status?**

Two possibilities:

- Stone Rides’ line: the **reason** for the circuit fee is simply to generate revenue and mirror sector norms, applied uniformly to all drivers. On that characterisation, the treatment is grounded in a neutral business model, not in Reeves’s part-time status; any disadvantage to part-timers is an incidental effect.
- Reeves’ line: the fee structure is linked to hours worked and availability — i.e. it is inherently designed with full-time utilisation in mind, and the financial detriment arises specifically **because** he works fewer hours (i.e. because he is part-time).

The key factual point the question gives us is that:

> Both sides agree that his status as a part-time worker was a factor…

Once we accept that part-time status **actually played a part** in the way the scheme operated on him compared with his full-time colleagues, and we adopt the proper legal test (an effective reason is enough), the causation requirement is satisfied:

- The less favourable effect (greater relative cost) arises because of his part-time status; that status is an operative factor when comparing him with a full-time comparator.

6. **Objective justification**

Under Regulation 5(2), Stone Rides can still avoid liability if it shows that the less favourable treatment is:

- Pursuing a **legitimate objective**; and
- A **necessary** and proportionate means of achieving that objective, on grounds other than part-time status.

Stone Rides’ proffered justification is:

- Generating revenue; and
- Aligning with sector norms.

Those can be legitimate objectives, but that is not the end of the inquiry; a court must consider whether:

- There are **less discriminatory alternatives** (e.g. commission-per-booking, sliding-scale or pro-rated fees) that would still allow sufficient revenue without imposing a substantially heavier relative burden on part-time workers.
- The blanket flat fee, knowing that it bites much more heavily on part-timers, is a proportionate way to achieve the revenue goal.

On the sparse facts given, Stone Rides has not shown:

- Why a flat fee is **necessary**, rather than merely convenient, and
- Why a more proportionate structure could not reasonably be adopted.

Mere reference to “sector norms” is generally insufficient by itself to demonstrate objective justification; courts routinely hold that “we do what everyone else does” and “it’s cheaper and simpler this way” are not, without more, enough to justify discriminatory effects where less discriminatory methods are reasonably available.

Given the burden is on the employer to prove justification, and given the availability in principle of alternative fee models that could generate revenue with less disparity for part-timers, an English court is likely to find that objective justification is **not** made out on these facts.

7. **Conclusion**

- Legally, under Regulation 5 and Directive 97/81 properly interpreted, Reeves does **not** need to prove that his part-time status was the **only** reason for the treatment complained of; it suffices that it was one effective reason.
- On the facts, both sides accept that his part-time status was indeed a factor.
- There is a credible basis to find less favourable treatment compared with full-time drivers, and Stone Rides has not, on the information provided, discharged the burden of proving objective justification.

Accordingly, an English court should find in favour of the claimant.

Under the Children Act 1989 and the Family Procedure Rules, the question for the court is not whether it *can* look into the death of Child R, but whether it *should* hold a discrete fact‑finding hearing about that death because doing so is **necessary and proportionate** to (a) deciding the s.31 threshold and (b) informing the welfare decision for Child S.

I’ll go through the legal framework and then apply it to the facts.

---

## 1. Legal framework

### (a) Threshold and welfare

- Under **Children Act 1989, s.31(2)**, a care order requires the court to be satisfied that the child:
  - is suffering, or is likely to suffer, significant harm, and
  - that this is attributable to the care given or likely to be given by the parent, or the child being beyond parental control.

- For **Child S**, the prior death of **Child R** with injuries sometimes associated with shaking/impact is potentially a key component of:
  - whether there is a *likelihood* of significant harm, and
  - whether Ms Samuels poses any ongoing non‑accidental injury risk.

- Once (and only once) threshold is crossed, **welfare is paramount** (s.1). But the *assessment of welfare and risk* often depends heavily on clear findings about past harm.

### (b) Role of past harm in predicting future risk

The case law is clear that:

- **Past facts matter**: Past harm is frequently the best available indicator of future risk.
  - See *Re H (Minors) (Sexual Abuse: Standard of Proof)* [1996] AC 563 and *Re B (Children)* [2008] UKHL 35: findings of past abuse can be used to establish a “likelihood” of future harm on the civil standard of proof.
- However:
  - You cannot assume future risk solely because someone was once in a “pool of possible perpetrators” (*Re J (Children)* [2013] UKSC 9). The court needs properly proved findings and a rational link to the new child.

Here, if it were proved on balance of probabilities that Ms Samuels caused or allowed the fatal injuries to Child R, that would be a powerful predictor of serious risk to Child S. If she is exonerated, the alleged non‑accidental element largely falls away. So the fact‑finding is not marginal; it goes to the core.

### (c) When should the court order a fact‑finding hearing?

The modern approach (including *Re H (A Child)* [2016] EWCA Civ 988 and similar authorities) is that:

- The court should conduct fact‑finding hearings **only where necessary** for:
  - determining the threshold, and/or
  - making properly informed welfare decisions.

Relevant factors typically considered:

1. **Seriousness of the alleged events** and their gravity.
2. **Relevance** of those allegations to the issues the court must decide about the current child.
3. The **quality and availability of evidence** – is a meaningful determination realistically possible?
4. The **impact on the timetable** and cost of the proceedings.
5. The **emotional and practical impact** on the parties, and
6. **Proportionality**: balancing Article 8 rights of the parent and child, and the state’s positive obligation to protect children.

So the question is not “must the court always investigate old events?” but “is a fact‑finding necessary and proportionate in this particular case?”

---

## 2. Application to these facts

### (a) Seriousness and centrality of the allegation

- The allegation concerns the **death of an infant** (Child R), with injuries of a kind sometimes linked to **shaking or impact trauma**.
- This is at the **highest end of seriousness** in family law; non‑accidental fatal injury represents extreme harm and risk.
- If it were proved that:
  - Ms Samuels inflicted those injuries, or
  - she failed to protect Child R from a known risk,
  that would be fundamentally determinative of risk to Child S.

This is not background “colour”; it is **potentially central** to the s.31 threshold and any ultimate welfare decision:

- If the court makes findings of non‑accidental involvement or failure to protect, that would substantially support the Local Authority’s case that Child S is “likely to suffer significant harm” in Ms Samuels’s care.
- If the court *does not* make such findings (and can affirmatively exclude Ms Samuels as responsible), the Local Authority’s position on risk is much weaker, and current good parenting may be more than sufficient to avoid any order.

Because the allegations are so grave and so directly tied to risk assessment, they strongly point toward a need for findings.

### (b) Availability and utility of evidence

- There has already been some level of previous investigation:
  - medical examination showing injuries of a type seen in possible shaking/impact trauma,
  - contemporaneous concerns about Ms Samuels’s anger, conflict at home, and drug use.
- There was **no criminal conviction**, but:
  - the family court applies the **civil standard of proof** (balance of probabilities),
  - absence of a conviction does *not* preclude a finding of non‑accidental injury if the civil standard is satisfied (*Re B*).
- The court can:
  - obtain and re‑analyse the medical records and expert evidence,
  - consider social work records, police material, and historical witness accounts.

While the passage of time makes fact‑finding more challenging, it does not render it futile. Courts often investigate historic injuries to siblings years later in care proceedings relating to a new child. Given:
- the existence of medical evidence,
- the extreme seriousness of the potential non‑accidental injury,
it is realistic to expect that a **meaningful** assessment may be made.

### (c) Relevance versus current good care of Child S

It is highly relevant that:

- Child S is currently **thriving** in Ms Samuels’s care, in a **residential assessment** with professional monitoring and support.
- This indicates that, in a supported environment, Ms Samuels is capable of providing good day‑to‑day care.

However, good current care does **not** by itself remove the necessity to explore a prior unexplained death where:

- the suspected mechanism (shaking/impact) may involve **episodic loss of control**, which may not be visible in routine observation,
- the alleged risks are of a **catastrophic** nature (serious brain injury or death),
- the child is again a very young, vulnerable baby, similar in age to the deceased sibling.

Many abusers of children function well and appear loving for long periods between episodes. Existing positive observations, especially in a structured, monitored setting, cannot safely be taken as conclusive that there is no underlying risk linked to unresolved past events of this gravity.

### (d) Proportionality, delay, and impact on Ms. Samuels

Ms Samuels’ objections are:

- A new investigation will be time‑consuming and resource‑intensive.
- It may emotionally destabilise her and impair her ability to concentrate on parenting Child S.
- The events are historic and were already looked at once (without prosecution).

These concerns engage:

- **Article 8 ECHR**: respect for family life, including avoiding unnecessary state interference and delay.
- **The overriding objective** (FPR r.1.1): dealing with cases justly, expeditiously, and in a way proportionate to the nature and importance of the issues.

Balanced against this are:

1. The **magnitude of potential risk**: an unassessed possibility that the same carer caused or failed to prevent a fatal injury to a previous baby.
2. The **State’s positive obligation** under Article 3/8 to protect children from serious ill‑treatment.
3. The fact that *not* making findings leaves both:
   - the court, and
   - the professionals
   operating under a cloud of uncertainty which could either:
   - expose Child S to unquantified lethal risk, or
   - unfairly stigmatise Ms Samuels without an attempt to resolve the issue.

In proportionality terms:

- Some delay and distress are **justifiable** where the court is dealing with whether there is a real prospect that Ms Samuels caused or allowed a previous child’s death.
- The necessary intrusion is directly connected to **protecting Child S**, not general character‑assessment or punishment.
- Moreover, clear findings—whether adverse or exonerating—are in the long‑term interests of both Child S *and* Ms Samuels. An unjustified suspicion hanging over her without determination may itself be a serious, indefinite interference with her Article 8 rights and prospects of parenting any child.

### (e) Necessity in the s.31 and welfare analysis

Without fact‑finding:

- The court must either:
  - discount the significance of Child R’s death (despite the medical evidence), or
  - treat it as a serious suspicion without proper proof.
- Either course is unsatisfactory:
  - Discounting it may under‑protect Child S.
  - Treating it as if proved without a dedicated fact‑finding hearing would be procedurally unfair and arguably a breach of Article 6 and 8.

With fact‑finding:

- The court can:
  - make clear, reasoned findings on the balance of probabilities about whether Child R’s injuries were inflicted, and if so by whom or within what pool,
  - use those findings transparently in assessing the likelihood of future harm to Child S, consistent with *Re B*, *Re S‑B*, and *Re J*.

Given the weight such findings would have on threshold and welfare, a fact‑finding hearing is not a luxuriously cautious option; it is **functionally necessary** to doing justice in the care proceedings.

---

## 3. Conclusion

Applying the established principles, an English court ought to decide that:

- A fact‑finding hearing into the circumstances of **Child R’s death** is **necessary and proportionate** to:
  - establishing the s.31 threshold regarding **Child S**, and
  - enabling a properly informed welfare evaluation.
- The gravity and centrality of the alleged past harm, and its direct potential impact on risk to Child S, outweigh the disadvantages of delay and emotional strain on Ms Samuels.
- Therefore, the Local Authority’s application for a fact‑finding hearing should be granted.

- Under reg 5(2), treatment is “less favourable” if:
  - it is on that ground; and
  - it is not objectively justified on grounds other than that the worker is part-time.
- Directive 97/81, cl 4(1), states part-time workers shall not be treated less favourably than full-time workers **“solely because”** they work part-time, unless justified on objective grounds.

So the case turns on (a) how to read “on the ground that…” / “solely because” in a mixed‑motive situation, and then (b) whether there is less favourable treatment and, if so, objective justification.

---

2. **Causation: must part-time work be the sole cause?**

(a) **Reading “solely because” in the Directive**

- If “solely because” were taken literally, any employer who could identify *any* additional motive (e.g. “to raise revenue” or “to follow industry practice”) could avoid liability, which would largely gut the protection.
- EU discrimination law (sex, race, etc.) interprets similar wording (“on grounds of”, “because of”) to mean that the protected ground must be an **effective or operative reason**, not the **only** reason. Mixed motives do not defeat a discrimination claim:
  - Analogous domestic authority: **Nagarajan v London Regional Transport [1999] UKHL 36** – “on racial grounds” is satisfied if race is a “significant operative cause”, not necessarily the only or even predominant one.
- The UK transposed “solely because” as “on the ground that the worker is a part-time worker” – language that mirrors other discrimination statutes and is naturally read the same way: part-time status must be an **effective cause** of the impugned treatment, not the exclusive cause.

An English court, applying the usual EU‑conforming approach to implementation, should therefore **reject a “sole cause” test** and adopt the established discrimination test: was Avalon’s part-time status **a real and substantial reason** for the treatment?

(b) **Application to the facts**

- The problem states that **“Both sides agree that his status as a part-time worker was a factor”** in how the fee scheme affected him; they just disagree about whether it was the *sole* basis.
- Under the correct legal test (effective cause, not sole cause), this is enough:
  - The fact Stone Rides also wanted to generate revenue or reflect sector norms does not negate that part-time status was an operative cause of the less favourable position into which the scheme placed part‑time drivers.
- On the causation issue alone, Avalon Reeves satisfies the statutory requirement: the less favourable position he complains of happened **on the ground, among others, that he was part‑time**.

---

3. **Is there “less favourable treatment”?**

(a) **Comparator**

- The obvious comparator is a **full‑time Stone Rides driver** doing the same work via the same booking system but working substantially more hours.
- Under reg 2(4), a part-time worker is comparable if they are employed by the same employer, under the same type of contract, engaged in the same or broadly similar work. That appears satisfied on these facts.

(b) **Nature of the fee and treatment**

- All drivers pay the same **flat “circuit fee”** for access to the booking system.
- In *form*, the contractual term is identical. But the PTW Regulations (and case law such as **British Airways plc v Pinaud [2021] UKSC 11**) look at whether, **in substance**, the part-time worker’s terms as a whole are less favourable, not just whether the wording is identical.
- Here, the practical effect is:
  - Full‑time drivers can spread the fixed fee over many more hours/ bookings, so the fee is a smaller cost proportionate to their earning opportunity.
  - Part‑time drivers, by definition, derive proportionately less use from the same access, so the fee constitutes a materially higher *per‑hour* or *per‑booking* cost.
- That is directly linked to the fact that Avalon and his comparators differ only in that he works fewer hours; the structure of the term systematically burdens part‑time drivers more heavily for the same facility.

On that analysis, an English court could properly find that, **as regards “terms of the contract” taken in context**, Avalon is being treated **less favourably** than full‑time drivers because the identical term does not operate on a pro rata or equivalent basis for him.

---

4. **Objective justification**

Once less favourable treatment on the ground of part‑time status is established, the employer can still avoid liability by showing **objective justification** (reg 5(2)(b), read with the Directive):

- Legitimate aim.
- Appropriateness and necessity (proportionality).

(a) **Stone Rides’ stated aim**

- Stone Rides argues the **principal reason** for the fee is to generate revenue and reflect sector norms – essentially, to cover the fixed costs of running the booking system in a commercially standard way.
- Cost-recovery and business viability are capable of being **legitimate aims** in EU/UK discrimination law, but *cost alone* is not normally sufficient; the employer must show that its means are proportionate and that a less discriminatory alternative would be inappropriate or would undermine the aim.

(b) **Proportionality of a flat fee**

- The fee is structured as a **flat amount per driver**, regardless of hours worked or bookings taken:
  - This is convenient administratively and predictable in income.
  - But it predictably and systematically hits part‑time drivers harder relative to their opportunity to benefit from the system.
- A court would ask:
  - Could the legitimate aim of cost‑recovery have been achieved by a **less discriminatory measure**, such as:
    - a pro‑rated fee linked to scheduled hours or average bookings; or
    - a lower “part‑time tier” fee combined with a higher full‑time fee; or
    - a small fixed fee plus a variable element per booking?
  - Is there evidence that such alternatives would be unduly complex, unworkable, or insufficient to meet the legitimate aim?
- On the facts given, Stone Rides offers only very broad justifications (“to generate revenue in line with sector norms”). There is **no evidence** of:
  - an attempt to design the scheme to avoid disproportionate impact on part‑time drivers; or
  - any real impediment to adopting a more proportionate, tiered or usage-based structure.

Given the directive’s clear protective purpose and the relatively straightforward availability of more proportionate models, an English court is unlikely to accept that a one-size-fits-all flat fee that bears clearly more heavily on part-time workers is **necessary** to achieve cost-recovery. The employer’s justification case looks underdeveloped and thin.

On the information provided, Stone Rides **has not discharged the burden** of showing that this less favourable treatment is objectively justified.

---

5. **Conclusion**

- The correct legal test under the PTW Regulations and Directive 97/81 does **not** require Avalon Reeves to prove that his part-time status was the **sole** reason for the less favourable treatment.
- It is sufficient that part-time status was an **effective, operative reason**, which is admitted on the facts.
- There is a plausible and, on these facts, persuasive finding of **less favourable treatment** when the fee’s actual effect on part‑time vs full‑time workers is assessed.
- Stone Rides’ business‑cost explanation is a legitimate aim in abstract but, on the information given, fails the **proportionality** test: the company has not shown that a flat, non‑pro‑rated fee is necessary or that less discriminatory alternatives would undermine its legitimate objective.

On this analysis, an English court should find for **Avalon Reeves**.

Avalon Reeves

Under the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) and prevailing U.S. contract principles, a court analyzing this dispute should focus on two core questions:

1. Can a nonsignatory ever enforce an arbitration clause?
2. If yes, do the specific relationships and allegations here put Jon Davidson within one of those accepted nonsignatory doctrines?

I’ll walk through that logic.

---

## 1. Legal framework: nonsignatories and the FAA

The FAA makes written arbitration agreements “valid, irrevocable, and enforceable” to the same extent as other contracts. It does not itself answer who, beyond signatories, can enforce these clauses.

The Supreme Court has made two key points:

- **State (or other applicable) contract law governs** who may enforce an arbitration clause.  
  - *Arthur Andersen LLP v. Carlisle*, 556 U.S. 624 (2009).
- Under such contract-law doctrines, **nonsignatories can sometimes compel arbitration**, including via:
  - agency,
  - veil-piercing / alter ego,
  - assumption,
  - third-party beneficiary status,
  - and various forms of equitable estoppel.
  - See *Thomson-CSF, S.A. v. Am. Arbitration Ass’n*, 64 F.3d 773 (2d Cir. 1995); *GE Energy v. Outokumpu*, 140 S. Ct. 1637 (2020).

So the right question is not “Did Davidson personally sign?” but “Does any recognized contract-law theory permit him, as a nonsignatory, to enforce this arbitration clause?”

---

## 2. The arbitration clause and scope

The contract between Harper Investors and Gold Reserve & Lending required arbitration of controversies “arising out of or relating to” the agreement.

That is a **broad** clause. Under federal law, such language is read expansively; disputes “touching matters” covered by the agreement generally fall within it unless expressly carved out.

All of Harper’s allegations are anchored in:

- the original **container leasing tax shelter investment**,  
- the ongoing administration and fallout of that program, and  
- Davidson’s later conduct “in connection with the container leasing program and related matters” and efforts to “help” investors who had been burned by that program.

Those disputes plainly “relate to” the original agreement.

So if Davidson is an eligible party to invoke the clause, the subject matter is within its scope.

---

## 3. Nonsignatory enforcement theories that fit these facts

Several well-recognized doctrines support Davidson’s ability to compel arbitration.

### A. Agency / officer / employee doctrine

Federal courts commonly allow corporate officers, directors, and employees to enforce arbitration clauses signed by the corporation when:

- the claims against them arise from the same facts as claims against the corporate signatory, and  
- their challenged conduct was undertaken in their corporate/agency capacity.

Examples:
- *Letizia v. Prudential Bache Securities, Inc.*, 802 F.2d 1185 (9th Cir. 1986): Brokerage employees allowed to invoke arbitration clause signed by the customer and brokerage.
- *Pritzker v. Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner & Smith, Inc.*, 7 F.3d 1110 (3d Cir. 1993): Affiliates and employees can rely on the firm’s arbitration clause for claims arising from the account relationship.

Here:

- Davidson became an **officer, director, and eventual owner** of Gold Reserve & Lending (by acquiring it through National Freight Consolidated).  
  - The corporate entity that originally signed with Harper Investors continued to exist; Davidson didn’t replace it, he controlled it.
- Harper’s own allegations tie Davidson’s actions directly to the ongoing container leasing program and Gold Reserve & Lending’s business.
- To the extent he used Gold Reserve & Lending (or successor structure) as the platform for his conduct, he was acting as its officer/agent.

Under agency principles, when the corporation can enforce an arbitration clause, courts frequently extend that right to its officers and agents for disputes arising out of that same contractual relationship. Otherwise, arbitration would become an empty formality, easily evaded by suing individuals instead of the entity.

**Result under this theory:** Davidson, as officer/owner acting on behalf of the signatory, can invoke the clause for conduct within that role.

---

### B. Successor / continuation of the contracting enterprise

Gold Reserve & Lending entered the contract; later Davidson, through National Freight Consolidated, purchased it and became its owner.

In a stock acquisition or similar ownership transfer:

- The corporation (Gold Reserve & Lending) remains the same legal person.
- Its **contracts, rights, and obligations** remain in place, including arbitration clauses.
- The new owner or controller steps into the role of directing the company’s performance of those obligations.

When Davidson later interacted with Harper Investors in the context of the same container leasing program originally sold by Gold Reserve & Lending, he was acting in furtherance of that same contractual enterprise.

Even if he did not personally sign the original contract:

- The signatory entity he now owns and manages did sign.
- The FAA and basic contract law favor enforcing the arbitration provision running with that continuing business relationship.
- To bar Davidson from invoking the clause while permitting the corporation to invoke it would elevate form over substance, given that his challenged acts arise from the same program.

**Result under this theory:** Because Davidson controls the signatory entity and the claims concern that entity’s contractual program, he stands in a position closely aligned with the corporate signatory’s rights under the arbitration clause.

---

### C. Equitable estoppel (“intertwined claims” doctrine)

Most circuits recognize some form of equitable estoppel that allows a nonsignatory to compel arbitration where:

1. The signatory’s claims against the nonsignatory are **“intimately founded in and intertwined with”** the underlying contract; and  
2. It would be inequitable to allow the signatory to both rely on the contract (or its benefits) and simultaneously avoid its arbitration clause.

See, e.g.:

- *MS Dealer Serv. Corp. v. Franklin*, 177 F.3d 942 (11th Cir. 1999);
- *Grigson v. Creative Artists Agency, L.L.C.*, 210 F.3d 524 (5th Cir. 2000);
- *Arthur Andersen LLP v. Carlisle*, recognizing estoppel as a valid state-law basis for nonsignatory enforcement.

Application to these facts:

- Harper Investors’ claims against Davidson are rooted in the **same investment relationship** created by the contract with Gold Reserve & Lending.
- The tax shelter program, its alleged fraudulent structure, and the subsequent “help” organizations (Fund Restoration Alliance, Tax Support Circle, etc.) all arise solely because of that original investment. But for that contract, none of this conduct would exist.
- The allegations describe a **single, continuing scheme** around that program: initial sale of the tax shelter, later efforts to address, modify, or “restore” value, and inducements not to sue—all tightly bound to the original contractual relationship and its fallout.

Harper is thus:

- Using the contractual transaction as the factual foundation of its claims,  
- While attempting to sidestep the arbitration mechanism that governs controversies “arising out of or relating to” that agreement.

That is exactly the situation in which courts have used equitable estoppel to let a nonsignatory enforce the clause.

**Result under this theory:** Because Harper’s claims against Davidson are intertwined with and derive from the contract, equitable estoppel supports allowing him to compel arbitration.

---

### D. Separate later entities (Fund Restoration Alliance, Tax Support Circle, Universal Business Services)

Harper may argue that Davidson’s later entities were separate from Gold Reserve & Lending and that some conduct occurred under new umbrellas, not as an agent of the original signatory.

Even so, two points cut in favor of arbitrability:

1. The **subject matter** of those activities is the same: dealing with the consequences of the container leasing tax shelter investment. That is still a “controversy … relating to” the original agreement.
2. The equitable estoppel doctrine looks to the **intertwining of facts and legal theories**, not just formal corporate names. Where the plaintiff’s claims against a nonsignatory depend on the same underlying transaction and alleged integrated scheme, courts generally still compel arbitration.

Unless Harper can genuinely isolate a discrete set of wrongs wholly independent from the tax shelter relationship (for example, an entirely different business transaction unrelated to the container leasing program), those additional entities don’t break the connection to the original arbitration agreement.

---

## 4. Effect of the default entered against Davidson

Harper obtained an order of default against Davidson while he was seeking to compel arbitration.

Important distinctions:

- An **entry of default** (often clerk’s default) is not the same as a **default judgment**. Courts have broad discretion to set aside an entry of default for “good cause.”
- Under FAA § 3, a court must stay litigation on any issue referable to arbitration upon application of a party “not in default in proceeding with such arbitration.”  
  - That “default” refers to failing to proceed with arbitration itself, not merely a procedural default in court.

Here, Davidson **actively sought arbitration**—he was not refusing to arbitrate. If his motion to compel was timely and he had not substantially participated in litigation on the merits, courts typically:

- Find **no waiver** of the right to arbitrate.
- Vacate the entry of default and send the dispute to arbitration, particularly given the strong federal policy favoring arbitration and resolving doubts in its favor.

Harper’s attempt to capitalize on the procedural default to defeat arbitrability is therefore weak under FAA principles.

---

## 5. Counterarguments for Harper Investors and why they likely fail

Harper can raise several objections:

1. **No signature by Davidson personally.**  
   - Rejected widely as dispositive; nonsignatories regularly enforce arbitration clauses under agency and estoppel doctrines.

2. **Claims sound in fraud and post-contract wrongdoing, not breach of contract.**  
   - But the clause covers disputes “relating to” the agreement, and courts routinely send fraud and securities/tax-shelter–type claims to arbitration when they arise from the investment relationship established by the contract.

3. **Later conduct via new entities is independent.**  
   - The factual connection and subject matter (rescue/aftermath of the tax shelter) remain grounded in the original program; the claims are intertwined with that contractual relationship.

4. **Equitable fairness: Davidson allegedly perpetuated fraud and should not benefit from arbitration.**  
   - The FAA and Supreme Court authority make clear that courts do not weigh the alleged merits or moral equities in deciding arbitrability; if the dispute falls within a valid arbitration clause and the nonsignatory can invoke it under contract law, the remedy is arbitration, not denial of that forum.

Overall, these arguments are unlikely to overcome the combined weight of agency, successor, and equitable estoppel doctrines favoring Davidson’s right to compel arbitration.

---

## 6. Who should prevail?

Applying federal arbitration policy and standard contract-law doctrines to these facts, a U.S. court should:

- Allow Jon Davidson, as an officer/owner and agent of Gold Reserve & Lending, and as part of the same intertwined scheme arising from the original investment contract, to **invoke the arbitration clause**;  
- Set aside the entry of default against him to the extent necessary; and  
- Compel arbitration of Harper Investors’ claims against Davidson as disputes “arising out of or relating to” the original agreement.

Thus, on the central legal issue—whether Davidson can compel arbitration as a nonsignatory—Davidson should prevail.

Under the federal estate tax, two core questions control whether Mary Winston’s estate can take a charitable deduction for the remainder to Elmwood University:

1. Does 26 U.S.C. § 2055(e)(3) even apply to this testamentary trust (i.e., is the charitable remainder a “reformable interest” under that subsection)?
2. If so, did the 1988 state‐court reformation produce a remainder that qualifies for a deduction under § 2055?

The Government prevails on both.

---

## 1. Statutory framework

### A. General charitable deduction and split‐interest rule

Section 2055(a) allows an estate tax deduction for bequests to charity, but § 2055(e)(2) sharply limits deductions for “split‐interest” transfers—where an interest passes to a noncharitable beneficiary (here, Kevin Fletcher for life) and the remainder passes to charity (Elmwood University).

Under § 2055(e)(2), if there is such a split interest, the charitable remainder is **not deductible** unless it takes one of a few prescribed forms (in substance):

- a charitable remainder annuity trust (CRAT),
- a charitable remainder unitrust (CRUT), or
- a remainder interest following a pooled income fund,

or the noncharitable interest is itself in a very specific, “qualified” form.

Mary Winston’s original trust, with broad payments and discretionary expenditures for Kevin Fletcher, does **not** fit any of these safe forms. It is a classic nonqualifying split‐interest trust under § 2055(e)(2).

### B. Reformation under § 2055(e)(3)

Congress created § 2055(e)(3) as a remedial provision. It allows certain nonqualifying split‐interest dispositions to be **judicially reformed** after the decedent’s death so that they retroactively satisfy § 2055(e)(2) and thereby qualify for a charitable deduction.

But the reformation relief is tightly cabined. It is available only for a **“reformable interest.”** Very roughly (without quoting), to be “reformable” under § 2055(e)(3)(C), the interest must:

1. Be a charitable remainder interest that fails the deduction **only** because it does not satisfy the CRAT/CRUT/pooled‐fund format of § 2055(e)(2);  
2. Arise under a governing instrument executed (or trust created) by a date Congress chose as a cutoff for this relief; and  
3. Not otherwise be disqualified under the general charitable deduction rules (e.g., the charitable remainder must still be “presently ascertainable” and not subject to a non‑negligible possibility of defeat under cases like *Ithaca Trust*, *Henslee*, etc.).

Harper Bank obtained a state‐court reformation in 1988, converting Kevin Fletcher’s interest into a fixed annual amount. This was done in order to “retrofit” the trust into a CRAT‑type structure. The success of that strategy for federal tax purposes turns entirely on whether the original remainder was a “reformable interest” in the statutory sense.

---

## 2. Execution date vs. codicil – does the testamentary plan qualify for the § 2055(e)(3) transition relief?

The key temporal dispute is:

- Harper Bank: The relevant “governing instrument” is Mary’s 1971 will, executed before the statutory cutoff. So the trust is grandfathered for purposes of § 2055(e)(3) relief.
- Government: A 1982 codicil materially altered Kevin Fletcher’s interests, and under ordinary will doctrine, that codicil **republished** the will as of 1982. Thus the governing instrument should be treated as executed after the cutoff date, placing it **outside** the class Congress was trying to protect.

### A. Effect of codicils in this context

Under traditional wills law, a codicil generally “republishes” the will, causing the entire will, as modified, to be treated as if executed at the date of the codicil—particularly for questions involving what law applies and how the dispositive provisions fit into that law.

Federal transfer tax cases have routinely looked to that doctrine when applying date‑based transition rules. Where Congress ties favorable treatment to the **date the governing instrument was executed or last amended**, courts typically treat a materially amended will as executed on the date of the **last codicil that affects substantive dispositive terms**.

Here:

- Mary executed the original will in 1971.
- She then executed codicils in 1972, 1977, and 1982.
- These codicils did not merely correct clerical errors; they “adjusted some details regarding Kevin Fletcher’s lifetime benefits.” Those adjustments directly affect the size and certainty of the eventual charitable remainder: more generous or more flexible benefits for the life tenant will generally reduce the value and predictability of the charity’s remainder.

Given that:

- The dispositive scheme involving Kevin and Elmwood University was actively reworked up through 1982.
- The federal statute’s more favorable treatment is keyed to whether the governing instrument is of a pre‑cutoff vintage.

A court applying standard republishing principles should treat the will as **re‑executed in 1982**. The governing instrument in force at Mary’s 1985 death is, in legal effect, a 1982 instrument.

### B. Legislative intent and fairness

The transitional reformation relief in § 2055(e)(3) is plainly aimed at **older instruments**—documents drafted before Congress imposed the CRAT/CRUT format, whose drafters could not reasonably have anticipated these technical requirements. Mary Winston’s dispositive plan does not fit that description:

- Her original will was executed **after** the 1969 tax reform that created the modern split‑interest rules.
- She continued to revise the lifetime benefits as late as 1982, long after the statutory environment was clear.
- She thus had many years and multiple codicil opportunities to structure Kevin’s interest in a qualifying CRAT/CRUT form if she wished to maximize the charitable deduction.

Strictly construing deductions as “matters of legislative grace,” and construing transitional relief in line with its policy goal, a court should not use § 2055(e)(3) to rescue a plan that was repeatedly and recently updated in a way that knowingly disregarded the safe harbors.

### C. Conclusion on the date issue

Because the 1982 codicil substantively altered Kevin Fletcher’s lifetime benefits and thus the actuarial remainder for Elmwood, the court should treat the governing instrument as executed in 1982. That is after the statutory cutoff for the more favorable treatment under § 2055(e)(3).

Result: the charitable remainder is **not** a “reformable interest” within the class Congress allowed to use post‑death reformation to obtain a deduction. On this ground alone, the Government should prevail.

---

## 3. Ascertainability of the charitable remainder – a second, independent problem

Even if a court were inclined to credit Harper Bank’s view on the effective execution date, there is a second fundamental obstacle: **the nature of Kevin Fletcher’s original interest.**

### A. General rule on ascertainability

Under longstanding case law and regulations (e.g., *Ithaca Trust Co. v. United States*, *Henslee v. Union Planters Bank*, *Merchants National Bank*, and Treas. Reg. § 20.2055‑2), a charitable remainder will be deductible only if:

1. The amount that will go to charity is **presently ascertainable** at the decedent’s death (i.e., it can be valued with reasonable certainty using actuarial methods); and  
2. The possibility that the charity’s interest will be defeated or reduced by the noncharitable beneficiaries’ rights is “**so remote as to be negligible**.”

If the trustee has broad, essentially open‑ended discretion to invade corpus for the noncharitable beneficiary, and no meaningful external standard cabins that discretion, then the charitable remainder is not considered presently ascertainable, and the deduction is denied.

### B. Scope of Kevin Fletcher’s rights under the original trust

The facts describe Kevin’s interest as including:

- Fixed monthly financial payments;
- Coverage of his medical expenses;
- Coverage of taxes;
- Upkeep and **improvements** on a specific Riverside residence; and
- Other expenditures on his behalf.

Crucially, the description emphasizes that these provisions “had the potential to reduce **unpredictably** the trust principal” that would go to Elmwood University.

Two features are problematic:

1. **Open‑ended improvements and expenses** – Funding “upkeep and improvements” to a residence, without any quantitative or objective cap, allows substantial capital expenditures that could consume large parts of the trust.  
2. **“Other expenditures”** – The presence of a broad residual category for “other expenditures” on Kevin’s behalf suggests the trustee’s authority is not confined to a tight, objectively determinable standard like “support in reasonable comfort,” but rather is more discretionary and expansive.

Given Kevin’s age (early 80s) at Mary’s death, some invasion was predictable: medical costs late in life can be significant, and capital upgrades to a residence can be very large. From the standpoint of the governing instrument at death, the range of possible invasions is too wide to say, with actuarial certainty, that the charity’s remainder is only negligibly at risk.

Under the regulations, one does **not** determine deductibility based on post‑hoc expectations about how the trustee will behave, but on the powers conferred by the instrument and the reasonable possibilities they create. The terms here authorize a level of discretionary spending that makes the principal available for Kevin’s benefit in ways that cannot be modeled with any reliable actuarial precision.

### C. Interaction with § 2055(e)(3)

Section 2055(e)(3) is designed to correct a **formal defect**—the failure of a split interest to be in the CRAT/CRUT/pooled‑fund format required by § 2055(e)(2)—where the underlying charitable remainder would otherwise be deductible.

If, however, the remainder fails the **separate, older** test of being presently ascertainable and not subject to a non‑negligible risk of defeat, then:

- The charitable remainder would be disallowed even if § 2055(e)(2) never existed.
- The failure is thus not “solely” a matter of improper form under § 2055(e)(2); it is a deeper substantive defect under the general § 2055(a)/regulatory doctrine.

Congress did not intend § 2055(e)(3) to rehabilitate fundamentally speculative remainders that would have been nondeductible under pre‑existing law. The definition of “reformable interest” is, by its structure and purpose, limited to those interests that would have qualified **but for** the technical CRAT/CRUT‑form requirement.

Here, because the trustee’s authority to expend principal for Kevin’s benefit (medical expenses, improvements, other expenditures) makes the remainder to Elmwood University insufficiently certain in amount at Mary’s death, the charitable interest is not “reformable” in the statutory sense.

So even if the court were to treat the will as a pre‑cutoff instrument for § 2055(e)(3) purposes (which it should not), **the breadth of the life tenant’s benefits still prevents the remainder from qualifying for a deduction after reformation.**

---

## 4. Overall conclusion

Putting the two key issues together:

1. **Execution date / codicil issue**:  
   - The 1982 codicil substantively altered Kevin Fletcher’s lifetime benefits and thus republished the will as of 1982.  
   - As a result, the governing instrument is treated as executed after the relevant cutoff date for § 2055(e)(3) transitional relief.  
   - The charitable remainder is therefore not a “reformable interest” eligible for that relief.

2. **Ascertainability issue** (independent ground):  
   - The original trust gave Kevin broad rights to payments and expenditures—including undefined improvements and “other expenditures”—that could significantly erode principal in unpredictable ways.  
   - This makes Elmwood University’s remainder not “presently ascertainable” and too uncertain to meet the long‑standing requirements for a charitable deduction.  
   - Because this is a substantive disqualifying feature, not merely a failure to adopt the CRAT/CRUT form, § 2055(e)(3) cannot cure it.

On either ground, and certainly when both are combined, the charitable remainder to Elmwood University does **not** qualify for the estate tax charitable deduction.

Accordingly, a U.S. court should rule in favor of the Government.

the Government

The question asks how an Irish court should interpret “public policy” in s.4(3)(j) of the Immigration Act 2004 and, in light of that interpretation, which side should win.

I’ll go through:

1. The statutory framework  
2. The competing interpretations of “public policy”  
3. Textual, contextual, and comparative arguments  
4. Application to the facts  
5. Overall conclusion on who should prevail  

---

### 1. Statutory framework: s.4 Immigration Act 2004

Section 4 governs “permission to land” for non-nationals at the Irish frontier. Subsection (3) lists grounds on which an immigration officer must refuse leave to land. Among them is:

- s.4(3)(j): refusal where the person’s entry or presence “could pose a threat to national security or be contrary to public policy” (paraphrasing the usual formulation).

The structure is:

- Multiple concrete, individualised grounds (e.g. no visa, insufficient funds, previous deportation).
- A residual/general ground: “national security or public policy”.

In practice, an immigration officer exercises **executive discretion** under statute, but that discretion must stay within the bounds of the Act and general public law (rationality, non-arbitrariness, consistency, etc.).

---

### 2. The competing interpretations of “public policy”

**Applicants’ (Zhao & Park’s) position**

- “Public policy” in s.4(3)(j) should be read narrowly.
- It must mean something akin to *ordre public*: a serious, individualised threat to core interests of the State (e.g. crime, extremism, significant risk to public order).
- It cannot be satisfied merely by the existence of some general governmental “policy” about immigration or education.
- On the facts, they are simply intending English-language students who pose no individual threat, and thus cannot be refused under s.4(3)(j).

**Minister’s position**

- “Public policy” is intended by the Oireachtas as a broad, open-textured concept allowing the State to run a coherent immigration system.
- It is not confined to individualised misbehaviour or threats; it can encompass general, prospective, and categorical policies (especially concerning the operation and integrity of visa/permission schemes).
- The published 2011 guidelines and the later Covid-era directives form a consistent “public policy” that:
  - Student permission is linked to bona fide in-person studies in Ireland; and
  - While courses are online-only due to Covid-19, there is a legitimate policy to refuse admission to new non-EEA language students whose courses have effectively become distance learning and who do not need to be physically present in Ireland.
- Acting in accordance with that policy falls within s.4(3)(j).

---

### 3. How should an Irish court interpret “public policy” in s.4(3)(j)?

#### (a) Textual reading

The phrase used is:

> “could pose a threat to national security or be contrary to public policy”

Points that favour the Minister’s broader reading:

- **Two distinct concepts**: “national security” and “public policy” are disjunctive.  
  - “National security” clearly captures serious, potentially individualised threats (terrorism, espionage, etc.).  
  - If “public policy” were limited to the same kind of grave individualised threats, it would add little; the legislature would not have needed both phrases.
- The legislature did **not** qualify “public policy” with adjectives like “serious” or “fundamental,” in contrast to EU formulations that carefully define such terms.
- In ordinary English (and Irish legal usage outside specialised EU law), “public policy” commonly refers to the State’s broader policy choices about the public good, including immigration control, economic policy, public health responses, etc.

This textual context makes it unlikely that “public policy” is confined only to individual wrongdoing or immediate, serious threats.

#### (b) Context within the 2004 Act

Section 4(3) includes several more mechanistic or categorical grounds for refusal, such as:

- No valid visa where one is required.
- Lack of documentary proof as to purpose of visit.
- Past deportation or exclusion.
- No ability to support oneself, etc.

These provisions show that the Oireachtas contemplated **categorical and prophylactic** refusals of entry, not only case-specific assessments of dangerousness.

A broad reading of “public policy” is consistent with that:

- It lets the executive adopt coherent **framing policies** for classes of entrants—e.g., rules on student migration, visitors from certain places, or restrictions driven by public health emergencies—so long as they are rational and applied consistently.

A narrow, EU-style “ordre public” reading (requiring serious individual threat) would:

- Significantly contract the practical utility of s.4(3)(j),
- And would not fit smoothly alongside the more administrative grounds elsewhere in the subsection.

#### (c) Relationship to EU law concepts

Under EU free movement law (e.g. Directive 2004/38/EC), restrictions on EU citizens and their families on grounds of “public policy”/“public security” must be based on:

- Personal conduct,
- Present and sufficiently serious threat,
- Affecting one of the fundamental interests of society.

But:

1. **Third-country nationals** (like these Malaysian applicants) are not exercising EU free movement rights. Their position is governed primarily by Irish domestic law, not by Directive 2004/38/EC.

2. The Immigration Act 2004 predates or at least is independent of that Directive framework and clearly has a different context: general immigration control at the frontier, not limitation of EU treaty rights.

3. Irish courts do often **draw analogies** from EU concepts, but they are not compelled to import the strict EU definition of “public policy” into a purely domestic immigration statute covering non-EEA nationals, especially where that would materially limit executive discretion that the Oireachtas appears to have deliberately conferred.

So while EU “public policy” jurisprudence is informative, it is not binding in this context and does not compel a narrow reading.

#### (d) Constitutional and institutional considerations

Immigration control at the border involves:

- High executive discretion,
- Rapid decision-making,
- Policy considerations ranging from labour market management to public health and resource constraints.

Irish constitutional jurisprudence has generally:

- Recognised a **wide margin of appreciation** for the executive in immigration control, particularly for people who have not yet been admitted to the State.
- Required that decisions be within the terms of the statute and subject to basic principles of fairness and rationality, but has not micro-managed immigration policy itself.

If a court were to hold that “public policy” in s.4(3)(j) can only arise where there is proof of individual dangerousness or something closely analogous:

- It would sharply **curtail** the ability of the Oireachtas and executive to implement forward-looking immigration strategies (e.g., limiting particular visa streams, exercising Covid-related controls).
- It would, in practice, constitutionalise a very narrow view of the public interest in immigration matters that the text does not clearly demand.

A more plausible constitutional approach is:

- Acknowledge that “public policy” in this context can include **general, non-individualised policy choices**, while subjecting their application to normal public law controls (non-arbitrariness, reasoned basis, non-discrimination, etc.).

---

### 4. Application of that interpretation to the facts

Assuming “public policy” can encompass general government immigration policy, the next question is whether **this** policy and its application qualify.

#### (a) The policy itself

Key elements:

- 2011 guidelines: non-EEA nationals are not to be admitted to Ireland as “students” where their proposed course exists only as a distance or online course.
  - This ties admission to the core rationale of the student scheme: physical study in Ireland and attendance at in-person classes.
- 2020 Covid-era directions: language schools were asked by the government to move classes online for public health reasons; prospective new students were warned that entry could be refused until in-person teaching resumed.

These measures serve recognisable public interests:

- Maintaining the integrity of the student immigration regime:  
  - If the studies are entirely online and can be done from abroad, there is little immigration justification for physical presence as a “student” in Ireland.
- Responding to the pandemic:  
  - Minimising non-essential inward travel during a public health emergency is an obvious element of public policy.

This is a classic example of **immigration policy** framed at a general level, combining education policy and public health objectives. It comfortably fits a broad reading of “public policy” in s.4(3)(j).

#### (b) Were the applicants treated in line with that policy?

On the facts given:

- They came to Ireland in December 2020 for an English course due to begin in January 2021.
- At that time:
  - Government had already moved such courses online.
  - Prospective students had been warned that entry before the resumption of in-person teaching might be refused.
- They were refused permission to land and directed to remain under supervision pending removal or voluntary departure.
- The refusal was grounded **specifically** on s.4(3)(j) and the policy that entry of new non-EEA language students for online-only courses would be contrary to the State’s public policy at that time.

There is no indication of arbitrariness or discrimination in their treatment as compared with others in the same position. The refusal is plainly and directly justified by the stated policy.

#### (c) Applicants’ main counter-arguments

1. **No individual threat**  
   - True, Zhao and Park posed no apparent personal risk to national security or public order in the narrow sense.
   - But under the interpretation above, **that is not necessary** for a refusal under “public policy”. The statute does not demand proof of personal dangerousness when the public policy ground is invoked.

2. **Policy allegedly too broad or insufficiently “public”**  
   - A policy that:
     - Maintains coherence of the student visa regime (linking physical presence to in-person study), and
     - Restricts non-essential travel and residence during a pandemic,
     is clearly connected to legitimate public interests (immigration control, public health, prudent use of State resources).
   - It is not irrational or capricious. It falls comfortably within the area that the Oireachtas could have expected “public policy” in s.4(3)(j) to cover.

3. **Procedural fairness / legitimate expectation** (implicit)  
   - If the applicants could prove they had been affirmatively misled or given formal assurances of admission despite the guidelines, there might be a separate argument about legitimate expectation; but the facts as presented emphasise that:
     - Government directives had already **warned** prospective students, and
     - The policy was both old (2011) and publicly available.
   - On those facts, there is no compelling fairness argument strong enough to outweigh a clear statutory ground being lawfully applied.

---

### 5. Overall conclusion

On a proper interpretation of s.4(3)(j):

- “Public policy” **does not** require proof of specific, harmful individual conduct or a grave threat akin to “national security”.
- It **can** encompass broader, generally applicable immigration policies, especially where:
  - They are rationally connected to recognised public interests (here, integrity of the student regime and Covid-19 health measures);
  - They are published and applied consistently.

Applying that to these facts:

- The Minister’s policy of refusing leave to land to non-EEA language students whose courses had been moved online-only during the pandemic falls well within “public policy” in s.4(3)(j).
- The immigration officer’s refusal to admit Zhao and Park in line with that policy was thus within statutory power.
- Accordingly, an Irish court should dismiss their challenges and uphold the refusals of permission to land.

1. **Legal framework**

Under the Refugee Convention, as applied in UK law, Mr Ho must show:

- A **well‑founded fear** (i.e. a “real risk” / “reasonable degree of likelihood”)  
- Of **persecution**  
- For a **Convention reason**: race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or membership of a particular social group  
- By the state or by non‑state actors in circumstances where the state is **unable or unwilling** to provide reasonable protection; and
- That it is not **reasonable to expect him to relocate** internally within Vietnam to avoid the risk.

Separately, for **Humanitarian Protection / Article 3 ECHR**, he must show a real risk of serious harm (e.g., torture, inhuman or degrading treatment) on return, again with no adequate state protection and no reasonable internal relocation alternative, but **without** the need for a Convention ground.

Credibility is assessed holistically, with s.8 of the Asylum and Immigration (Treatment of Claimants, etc.) Act 2004 providing that certain behaviours (notably late claims) must be taken as **damaging credibility**, though they are not automatically decisive.

2. **Issues to be decided**

On these facts, an English court would need to decide:

1. Is Mr Ho’s core account about persecution related to military service and bribe‑demanding aggressors **credible**?
2. If so, does it engage a **Convention ground** (e.g. political opinion or particular social group), or is it simply criminal extortion / corruption?
3. Is the Vietnamese state **unable or unwilling** to protect him from those aggressors?
4. Could he **reasonably relocate** within Vietnam to avoid the risk?
5. Even if he does not qualify as a refugee, does he qualify for **Humanitarian Protection / Article 3**?

3. **Credibility under s.8 and general principles**

Factors undermining Mr Ho’s credibility:

- **Very late asylum claim**:  
  - He arrived clandestinely (effectively) by leaving a cruise ship in the UK.  
  - He stayed, worked illegally (or at least without immigration status), and was convicted for involvement in cannabis production.  
  - He did *not* claim asylum until removal/deportation action was initiated.  
  Under **s.8 AITCA 2004**, that is a classic, strongly adverse factor. Tribunals repeatedly say that making a claim only when facing removal “significantly damages” credibility, absent compelling explanation.

- **Inconsistencies / lack of documentation**:  
  - He says he was repeatedly forced to pay bribes and physically assaulted.  
  - He offers **no documentary evidence** of payments or attempts to complain, despite alleging long‑running, serious extortion.  
  - He has not shown any formal complaint to higher authorities, party officials, or other state bodies.

- **Objective evidence about military exemption**:  
  - The Secretary of State relies on **official documents showing his father had recognised ‘martyr’ status and that this gave Mr Ho an exemption from military service**.  
  - That tends to undermine the central plank of his narrative that he was seriously at risk because of *non‑compliance with military service obligations*.

Factors supporting his credibility:

- **Medical evidence from River Clinic and Maple District Hospital** in Ho Chi Minh City:  
  - They appear to show that Mr Ho *did* suffer injuries in Vietnam around the relevant period.  
  - His explanation—that he lied to hospital staff about the cause of the injuries due to fear of his aggressors—is not inherently implausible in a corrupt or authoritarian context.
  - Under established case law, such medical evidence can corroborate **that injuries occurred**, but usually does not by itself establish **who caused them or why**.

- **Plausibility of local corruption**:  
  - It is well‑documented that Vietnam, like many states, has areas where **local corruption and informal power networks** are real; it is not inherently implausible that someone would be extorted for money, including under the pretext of military service issues.
  - The fact that a person is formally exempt from service does not *wholly* exclude the possibility of corrupt officials ignoring that exemption.

A tribunal applying UK law will generally:

- Accept that **some injuries occurred** in Vietnam, but  
- Ask whether the evidence is strong enough to accept Mr Ho’s full account about *who* attacked him, *why*, and *with what consequences*.

On the limited facts given, the adverse factors (late claim; contradictory military‑service narrative; no complaint to other authorities; no corroborating evidence of the alleged extortion; economic migration profile) are likely to **outweigh** the partial support from the medical evidence.

4. **Convention reason**

Even taking Mr Ho “at his highest” (i.e. assuming his core narrative is broadly true):

- His claim is essentially that:
  - Certain individuals (apparently with some local power) **extorted annual bribes** from him and assaulted him,
  - Using his supposed military obligations (despite his father’s martyr exemption) as a lever.

For a **Refugee Convention** claim, he must show that the harm is “for reasons of” a Convention ground:

- **Political opinion**:  
  - There is no clear evidence Mr Ho was targeted *because of* oppositional political opinion or activity.  
  - Rather, he was allegedly targeted as **someone perceived as able to pay** or as a convenient victim.  
  - If he had resisted on anti‑corruption grounds and that resistance had been perceived as political opposition to the regime or party, there could be an arguable political‑opinion angle.  
  - But nothing in the summary suggests the tribunal is being asked to accept that. The narrative is framed as ad hoc extortion, not political dissent.

- **Particular social group**:  
  - Being the son of a martyr might, in some circumstances, be a social category, but here it is **protective** (it grants exemption) rather than the reason for persecution.  
  - There is no suggestion he was being targeted *because* he belonged to a stigmatised group; instead, the martyr status theoretically benefitted him.

On these facts, a court is likely to find **no Convention nexus**, even if some harassment occurred. That alone would defeat the asylum claim, even assuming credibility.

5. **Sufficiency of protection**

If the persecutors are **non‑state actors** (corrupt local officials, criminal networks, etc.), Mr Ho must show the **Vietnamese state is unable or unwilling to provide a reasonable level of protection**.

- The material given shows:
  - No real attempt by Mr Ho to **seek protection** from higher/Vietnam‑wide authorities or anti‑corruption channels, or from police outside the immediate circle of those he accuses (if they are local officials).
  - No evidence that he would be of **adverse interest at a national level**, or that escalation beyond his local area would be futile or dangerous.
- General country information (as typically taken into account by UK tribunals) indicates:
  - Vietnam has problems with corruption and local abuses, but  
  - It is not a failed state, and there is at least a **baseline of law enforcement** and functional government structures.

Tribunals often hold that absent strong evidence of systemic inability or unwillingness to protect someone in his position, a claimant cannot meet the threshold. On the given facts, the court would almost certainly conclude:

- Even if localised corruption / abuse existed, Mr Ho has **not shown** that the Vietnamese state overall would be unable or unwilling to protect him if he complained **outside** his persecutors’ area of influence.

That undercuts both any Refugee Convention claim and any Art 3/Humanitarian Protection claim.

6. **Internal relocation**

Even if some localised risk in his home area were accepted:

- Mr Ho could, on the evidence, **relocate within Vietnam**, particularly to another city or province, to avoid the aggressors.
- There is no evidence that:
  - The persecutors have nationwide reach; or
  - He is on any national “wanted” list; or
  - He would face destitution or conditions amounting to Article 3 ill‑treatment if he resettled elsewhere in Vietnam.

Given his age, prior capacity to work on an international cruise ship, and lack of evidence of any special vulnerability, it is highly likely a tribunal would find **internal relocation reasonable**.

7. **Effect of criminality and late claim**

While his cannabis‑production conviction does not in itself make him ineligible for protection (it is highly unlikely to trigger Refugee Convention exclusion as a “particularly serious crime” in the sense used in Art 33(2)), it is relevant in two ways:

- It reinforces the picture of Mr Ho as someone whose **primary motive** in coming to and staying in the UK was **economic** rather than protection‑related.
- When combined with his **failure to claim asylum until deportation**, it powerfully supports the Secretary of State’s argument under **s.8 AITCA 2004** that his account has been **manufactured or embellished** only to avoid removal.

Courts are cautious not to treat criminality as automatic evidence of lying. Nonetheless, in the overall credibility assessment, this is an adverse contextual factor.

8. **Overall assessment**

Pulling the strands together:

- **Credibility**: On the facts as presented, an English court is likely to find Mr Ho’s account **not sufficiently credible** to meet even the “reasonable degree of likelihood” threshold. The late claim, conflict with objective evidence about military exemption, failure to seek help from authorities, and lack of corroboration for long‑term extortion outweigh the partial corroboration provided by medical records.
- **Convention ground**: Even if partially believed, the harm described is more consistent with **private extortion / corruption** than persecution for a Convention reason. 
- **State protection and relocation**: There is no adequate evidence that Vietnam cannot or will not protect him, nor that he could not safely and reasonably **relocate internally** to another part of the country.

On this basis, an English court/tribunal should dismiss the asylum and humanitarian protection claims and uphold the Secretary of State’s decision to deport.
